Opening: On a surface with two handles, how far can one twist move a loop?
A whole loop is one vertex. Two vertices share an edge if their loops can be drawn disjointly.
Distance counts the fewest of these moves. Drawing six edges leaves a question. Could five have worked?
Collar: Start with two loops, A and B, that cross twelve times and sit four edges apart.
To twist A around B, open a thin collar into a strip. Its left and right sides match.
Keep the bottom still and slide the top one full turn. Watch a strand leave on the right and reappear on the left.
Each of twelve moving strands crosses each of twelve fixed strands. One twist gives a hundred and forty-four crossings. Two give two hundred and eighty-eight.
Mahanta proved that one twist of this particular pair gives distance five. What happens at two twists?
Fold: Take a shortest path of four edges from A to B. Stop one step early, at W.
W misses B, so twisting around B fixes W.
Copy the first three edges, twist the copy, and attach it in reverse. Three edges out, three edges back.
This gives six moves to the twisted loop. To prove the distance, we have to rule out every shortcut.
Bounds: Try four twists first. Imagine lifting the path into an annular cover around B. When every loop crosses B, each edge can advance at most one step there.
Four twists put the projected ends six steps apart. Five edges cannot span that gap.
And if the path visits a loop that misses B, reaching that loop costs at least three moves from either end. Again, six.
Now turn the dial down to two twists. The projected gap falls to four. A five-edge shortcut is still possible on this evidence.
Search: Here is how to finish. Cut along A, and triangulate. The crossing counts on the sides of a triangle tell us how the strands connect inside.
An efficient-geodesic theorem says that if a shortcut exists, a shortest one starts with bounded crossing counts. We can test a finite list.
For the double twist, there are eighty candidate first moves. Following them produces fourteen thousand and sixteen terminal tests.
Every terminal pair fills the surface with disks. No essential loop misses both. Every proposed shortcut fails.
So the answer for this drawing is exact. One twist gives five. Two twists, three twists, and every higher power give six.
Census: Could a single twist ever get all the way to six? Change the starting pair, but keep its distance at four.
Twelve crossings is the minimum on the double torus. There are five kinds of ordered starting pairs at that size. Every one twists to distance five.
At thirteen crossings there are eleven kinds. Again, every one twists to five. So a pair can give five without having minimum intersection.
At fourteen crossings, one pair finally reaches six. The two resulting curves cross a hundred and ninety-six times.
Fourteen is therefore the smallest starting count that works for this one-twist construction. The minimum over all distance-six pairs is a separate question.
AnyDistance: Curves at every distance were known long before this calculation. Here is how the general idea works.
With enough twists, fold a length-four geodesic into one of length six. Fold again and its length is ten.
Stop seven edges along that path. Any shortcut to that point would shorten the whole path. So those two vertices are exactly seven apart.
The short-twist result answers a more precise question. For Mahanta's drawing, two turns suffice. With the right fourteen-crossing starting pair, one turn does it.
